questions.q: How does this lesson define governance in the enterprise Salesforce sense?
options: A single person's informal habit of reviewing changes before they go live
The set of standing decisions, standards, and decision rights that keep a platform coherent as it grows
A one-time audit performed when a company first implements Salesforce
A technical feature built into the Salesforce platform itself
questions.explain: Governance is defined as a deliberate operating model -- standing decisions, standards, and decision rights -- that prevents drift as more teams, integrations, and customizations are added over time, not an informal habit.

questions.q: What does this lesson describe a Center of Excellence (CoE) as?
options: A single external consultant hired once per year
A cross-functional team combining platform specialists and business stakeholders that owns the platform's standards and direction
A Salesforce Trailhead badge earned by completing modules
An automated monitoring tool with no human members
questions.explain: The lesson describes a CoE as cross-functional, combining platform specialists (admins, developers, architects) with business stakeholders, owning standards and direction rather than any one team's local interests.

questions.q: What specific failure mode does this lesson warn a Center of Excellence can fall into?
options: Becoming too technically skilled to communicate with business stakeholders
Becoming a slow approval board that blocks every request instead of making a short list of key decisions quickly
Having too few meetings to be effective
Only being allowed to exist in companies with a single Salesforce org
questions.explain: The lesson's explicit warning is that a CoE can become a bottleneck -- a slow approval board over everything -- rather than the useful version, which centralizes only a short list of genuinely important decisions and lets everything else move at the team's own speed.

questions.q: Which of the following does this lesson list as an example of a decision that commonly needs centralized governance?
options: What font a sales rep uses in their personal email signature
The data model, integration architecture, security model, and release process
Which color theme an individual user selects for their own Salesforce profile
What time of day an individual user logs in
questions.explain: The lesson cites the data model, integration architecture, security model, and release process as commonly-centralized decisions, while everything else is left to move at the pace of the team doing the work.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why does a System Architect have a direct interest in a governance body having real decision rights?
options: Because without an authoritative body to make and hold decisions like system-of-record assignment or org strategy, the architect's own recommendations have nowhere authoritative to land
Because governance bodies are solely responsible for writing Apex code
Because a System Architect's role is made unnecessary once a CoE exists
Because decision rights have no bearing on technical architecture work
questions.explain: The lesson explains that decisions like system-of-record assignment, integration standards, master data ownership, and org strategy need a governance body with real authority -- otherwise a System Architect's well-reasoned recommendations have no mechanism to actually be enforced.
